title: Our Mutual Friend: A Literary Discussion

segments.title: Opening: Money, Dust, and the Thames

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked — a close reading of Charles Dickens's last completed novel.
This is a book about money — who has it, who wants it, who is destroyed by wanting it.
It's a book about the Thames — dark, tidal, indifferent — and about a society that measures human worth in dust heaps and inheritance.
Over the course of this series, we'll be reading the novel passage by passage, arguing about what it means, and trying to understand why it still matters.
With me today are three guests, each of whom brings something essential to this conversation.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don — a man who has spent a lifetime reading novels as moral documents, as tests of individual character and conscience.
He will keep us honest when we are tempted to turn Dickens into something simpler than he is.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian whose speciality is precisely the world this novel inhabits — the Poor Law, the river trade, the institutions of Victorian London.
He will tell us what it actually felt like to be poor in this world — and why that matters for reading the book.
And Oliver Trevelyan — actor, writer, and the man who has read more classic novels aloud than anyone alive — brings the performer's ear.
He hears things in Dickens's prose that the rest of us miss when we read in silence.
Let's begin with the novel's great subject — the body in the river, the dead man who isn't dead, and what Dickens does with money and identity from the very first pages.
The first thing to observe about this novel is how completely Dickens has organised it around a single, extraordinarily potent image.
A man presumed dead, whose fortune depends on that death, who must choose whether to return to life and inherit — or remain a ghost.
That is not a social thesis. That is a moral situation of the highest order — worthy of Shakespeare, I would venture.
And Dickens does not squander it. The river is not merely atmospheric backdrop — it is the very element in which identity dissolves and must be recovered.
Edmund's point about identity is well-taken, and I think the novel earns it precisely because Dickens anchors it in something historically exact.
The Thames in the 1860s was a working river — it carried bodies, real ones, with terrible regularity.
The river police, the body-finders, the inquest system — these were functioning institutions, and Dickens knew them.
What strikes me in the John Harmon passages is how precisely the horror is located — it isn't supernatural. It is administrative.
Harmon reads about his own death in a government placard posted at Whitehall. The state has certified him dead.
Dickens gives us the moment of drowning consciousness first, and it is extraordinary — listen to this passage.
"This is John Harmon drowning! John Harmon, struggle for your life. John Harmon, call on Heaven and save yourself!"
The self addresses the self in the second person — as if identity can only be recovered by speaking one's own name back to oneself.
That is not the rhetoric of melodrama. That is something much stranger and more precise.
James has put his finger on exactly what makes that passage remarkable to read aloud — and believe me, I have read it aloud.
The repetition of "John Harmon" three times — it's almost liturgical. You can't rush it.
Dickens has written stage directions into the grammar itself. The exclamation mark, then the comma, then the imperative — each one a beat.
And then he follows it with the murder of Radfoot — which is told with this extraordinary cold economy, almost a legal summary.
Harmon says, and here I must quote it directly, that —

"Radfoot had been murdered by some unknown hands for the money for which he would have murdered me, and that probably we had both been shot into the river from the same dark place into the same dark tide."
"The same dark place into the same dark tide" — that repetition is Dickens doing something almost Biblical. It's the cadence of fate.
Two men, one fortune, one river. The novel's entire moral universe is already present in that sentence.
Oliver is quite right about the cadence — and I would add that this is precisely the kind of effect one cannot achieve by paraphrase.
The critics who want to read Our Mutual Friend as social polemic tend to paraphrase it into something much flatter.
What Dickens has written is a story about what money does to the soul — which is a different thing entirely from a story about what money does to society.
John Harmon, at the bottom of the Thames, fighting to speak his own name — that is a scene about the self, not the system.
I'd resist that dichotomy slightly, Edmund — because the system is precisely what makes the self uncertain here.
Harmon's identity has been confiscated by an inheritance law. He is dead on paper because the law and the money have conspired to make him so.
And Dickens is sharp enough to see that even the novel's satirical grotesques carry the same burden — the Wegg passages make this wonderfully clear.
There's a passage where the stuffed specimens in Wegg's lair seem to pass sardonic judgment on human greed.
"The yard or two of smile on the part of the alligator might have been invested with the meaning, 'All about this was quite familiar knowledge down in the depths of the slime, ages ago.'"
The alligator has seen it all before. Greed, envy, ingratitude — they are older than civilisation, and the slime knows it.
Dickens is doing both things at once — the moral and the social — and I think that is what makes this novel inexhaustible.
The alligator is one of my favourite characters in English fiction, and he doesn't move a muscle.
That is Dickens's comic genius at its most controlled — he gives more life to a stuffed reptile than most novelists give to their protagonists.
And James is absolutely right — the alligator's ancient cynicism about human nature is the novel's key note, sounded very early.
Money corrupts, greed betrays, the river takes — and the slime was there before any of us and will be there after.
The slime, the tide, the alligator's ancient smile — Dickens has set up a world that reaches back before human institutions and forward past all of us.
In our next segment, we'll turn to the characters who make their living from that river — and what it costs them.

segments.title: Bella's Reckoning: From Mercenary to Moral

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.

I'm your host, and today we're examining one of the novel's most contested arcs — the transformation of Bella Wilfer from what she herself calls a mercenary little wretch into something altogether finer.
With me are three guests whose perspectives I suspect will both illuminate and occasionally collide.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don whose lifelong conviction is that the great novelist's genius lies in moral imagination — in showing us what goodness actually costs.
Professor James Blackstone brings the historian's eye — he knows what the institutions really were, what poverty meant, and why the law shaped lives in ways we can still recognise.

And Oliver Trevelyan — actor, writer, and the voice behind more classic-novel audiobooks than anyone alive — reads every page as a performer and hears what the prose is doing before anyone else in the room.
Let's begin with the emotional foundation Dickens lays beneath Bella's story — a memory, a child by a fire, and a woman who wished she could run away with him.
What Dickens gives us in Mr Boffin's account of young John Harmon is something quite beyond sentiment.
It is the novel's first insistence that there was a moral debt contracted long before any of the plot's mechanics began to turn.
Boffin speaks in the vernacular, but Dickens is composing something closer to elegy.
Listen to how he sets the scene:
"There was his little scanty travelling clothes upon him. There was his little scanty box outside in the shivering wind, which I was going to carry for him down to the steamboat."
That doubled word — scanty, scanty — does extraordinary work.
It is the repetition of a man who cannot quite bring himself to move past the image.
And then Mrs Boffin kneels, warms her hands, rubs the child's cheeks — and the tenderness tips over into something she cannot contain.
The moral texture of everything that follows — including Bella's own test — is embedded in that single scene.
Edmund is right about the doubling, and I'd go further — this is a passage written to be spoken aloud.
Boffin's syntax is almost musical — it lurches, it repeats, it strains under the weight of what he's carrying.
And then comes the line that stops everything:
"I'd give the wide wide world, I would, to run away with him!"
That redundancy — wide wide world — is not careless writing.
It's the sound of a woman whose grief has overwhelmed the capacity of ordinary language.
Every time I read that line — and I've read it rather more times than most people — it lands exactly the same way.
I want to hold that image a moment longer, because there's something Dickens is being precise about which a modern reader might miss.
The old man — Harmon senior — won't allow sixpence for coach-money to get this seven-year-old to the steamboat.
Sixpence.
This is a man who will die one of the wealthiest in London, and he begrudges his son the price of a short cab ride.
The whole novel's moral argument about what money does to its possessors — and to the children of its possessors — is contained in that single withholding.
Which is exactly why John Harmon, when he has the chance to step back from his inheritance, does so.
And that brings us directly to Harmon's extraordinary decision — to remain, as it were, dead.
To use the danger he has survived not merely as a disguise, but as a kind of moral instrument.
The plot mechanics here are worth pausing over, because they are stranger and more troubling than they first appear.
Harmon and Radfoot — two men who could pass for each other — hatch a scheme on the voyage to England:
"the plot was made out of our getting common sailors' dresses, and throwing ourselves in Bella Wilfer's neighbourhood, and trying to put ourselves in her way."
Now, a legal historian notes something quietly alarming here.
Harmon has been assigned a wife by his father's will — a woman who had no say in the matter — and his first impulse is to observe her in secret before deciding whether to claim her.
There is something genuinely uncomfortable about a man who frames surveillance as chivalry.
I take Blackstone's point — and it is not a point to be dismissed — but I think it mistakes the novel's moral register.
Harmon himself is perfectly clear about what drives him, and it is not vanity or control.
It is fear — specifically, a fear rooted in what his father's money had already destroyed.
He says — and one must hear this carefully:

"The dread of our being forced on one another, and perpetuating the fate that seemed to have fallen on my father's riches — the fate that they should lead to nothing but evil — was strong upon the moral timidity that dates from my childhood with my poor sister."
That phrase — moral timidity — is one of the most precise pieces of self-knowledge in the novel.
Harmon is not a schemer; he is a damaged man trying, imperfectly, to avoid repeating damage.
Both things can be true simultaneously, which is rather how Dickens works.
The plot is ethically wobbly and the man inside the plot is genuinely trying to do right.
What interests me as a performer is the theatrical audacity of it — dead man walks, watches from the wings, decides who gets to know he's alive.
Dickens has written a protagonist who is, structurally, a ghost for most of the novel.
And what this ghost is watching — with particular attention — is whether Bella will sell herself for comfort, or whether there is something else in her.
And the world around Bella, of course, is not exactly designed to bring out the finer impulse.
Dickens is meticulous about the degradation that surrounds those who might have risen — or might yet fall further.
The passage Lizzie speaks about Jenny Wren's father is almost clinical in its precision, and the more devastating for it.
She says of the child:
"This poor ailing little creature has come to be what she is, surrounded by drunken people from her cradle — if she ever had one, Charley."
That parenthetical — if she ever had one — is a masterpiece of compression.
It says: this child may not have had even the most basic material comfort of infancy.
And the father is described with extraordinary ambivalence — weak, wretched, falling to pieces, never sober, but — and Dickens insists on this — a good workman at his actual work.
The novel refuses to flatten its poor into simple victims or simple failures.
That ambivalence you identify is everywhere in this book, James, and it's one of the reasons it rewards a performer.
Nobody in the novel is purely one thing — and that includes Bella, who begins by being quite honestly awful about money.

Which is rather brave of Dickens — to make the character we're meant to root for someone who, in her early chapters, would absolutely have married for wealth if the opportunity had presented itself properly.
The transformation only means something because the starting point was genuine.
This is precisely where I would locate the novel's moral achievement — and I use that word without apology.
Bella does not drift into goodness.
She chooses it — chooses poverty over the gilded life that Boffin's fortune had begun to offer her — and goes to her father.
R. Wilfer's response is one of the finest things in the book — and Dickens gives him a rhetoric worthy of the occasion:
"The mercenary young person distantly related to myself, did well! The mercenary young person distantly related to myself, did not trust to me in vain!"
And then — this is the turn that makes it something more than comedy:
"she brings you a good fortune when she brings you the poverty she has accepted for your sake and the honest truth's!"
Poverty as fortune — that is the novel's central paradox, and Wilfer articulates it with absolute conviction.
The threefold repetition of mercenary young person distantly related to myself — I mean, it's a gift.
Wilfer is using the language that was used against Bella — and against him — and reclaiming it as a banner.
He's the gentlest man in the novel, and here, for one glorious moment, he gets to be the most eloquent.
There is a nice irony in the fact that the novel's most biting satire on wealth and its pretensions falls to Mr Boffin — himself newly rich.
His attack on the charity-patron machinery is wonderfully precise:

"Patrons and Patronesses, and Vice-Patrons and Vice-Patronesses, and Deceased Patrons and Deceased Patronesses, and Ex-Vice-Patrons and Ex-Vice-Patronesses, what does it all mean in the books of the Charities that come pouring in on Rokesmith as he sits among 'em pretty well up to his neck!"
The accumulation — patron, vice-patron, deceased patron, ex-vice-patron — enacts the very absurdity it mocks.
And this is the world from which Bella is extricating herself — a world where giving five shillings to a charity entitles you to a title and a place in the annual report.
Her choosing Rokesmith and poverty over all of that is a direct rebuke to the entire system.
I would add only this: the rebuke works because it is personal, not programmatic.
Dickens does not give us a heroine with a social theory.
He gives us a woman who, at a particular moment, in a particular room, makes a particular choice — for love, for honesty, and for the man she has come to see clearly.
That is how moral imagination operates in the novel — not in argument, but in action.
Moral imagination in action — that's a phrase worth sitting with as we move forward.

Bella's arc, we've seen, runs from the child by Boffin's fire — present in memory but absent in fact — through disguise, observation, and charity-list satire, to a father's blessing that redeems the very word mercenary.
Our next segment turns to the novel's other great transformation — the river itself, and what Dickens does with dust, water, and the relentless motion of things between the living and the dead.

segments.title: The Dust Heaps and Social Corruption

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the programme that takes Dickens's last completed novel apart piece by piece to see what's inside.
I'm joined today by three remarkable minds who bring very different lenses to this extraordinary book.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don and lifelong champion of the novel as a moral art form — for him, Dickens matters because individual character matters.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who knows exactly what it meant — in hard institutional fact — to be poor in Victorian England.
And Oliver Trevelyan has read more Dickens aloud than almost anyone alive — he hears the rhythms, the comic timing, the theatrical architecture of every sentence.
Today we're in the thick of what I think is the novel's central obsession: the Dust Heaps, the money they represent, and what that money does to people.
We'll be asking what Dickens actually believes about wealth, charity, corruption — and about whether goodness can survive in a world built on refuse.
The Dust Heaps are not a metaphor Dickens invented from whole cloth — they were real, vast, and enormously profitable.
The mounds of accumulated filth on the northern fringes of London represented exactly the kind of fortune that Victorian England found it convenient not to examine too closely.
And what Dickens does with that inheritance — what he shows flowing toward Boffin the moment his wealth becomes public — is a catalogue of social parasitism so precise it reads like a legal record.
He gives us the Secretary opening letters — and the sheer volume of what pours in is the satire.
Listen to this: Dickens writes,
'Oh the varieties of dust for ocular use, offered in exchange for the gold dust of the Golden Dustman!'
Gold dust in exchange for ocular dust — the whole novel is in that one sentence.

Every fraudulent charity, every lithographed ducal letter, every 'dear sir' addressed to Boffin by a peer who cannot be bothered to write the name by hand — it is all dust offered back in place of gold.
And he cannot resist actually giving us the letter — in full — from the Duke of Linseed.
The postscript is the masterpiece: 'The Steward's fee is limited to three Guineas.'
'Thoughtful in the postscript,' Dickens adds — and that dry parenthesis is worth a paragraph of analysis on its own.
What delights me as a performer is that the prose is performing the very thing it describes.
It has the shape and pomposity of the duke's own letter — and then punctures it.
Dickens is doing exactly what every great comic writer does — he adopts the voice of the thing he despises and lets it convict itself.
One would not wish to dampen the comic pleasure — and it is genuine pleasure — but I think there is a risk of reading these passages as merely satirical.
What Dickens is doing is more uncomfortable than satire.
He is showing us that the arrival of money does not simply attract the corrupt — it exposes something already there, latent, in human nature.
The individual beggars in the following passage are particularly devastating on this point.
Dickens writes that
'they call their scraps documents; but they are, as to papers deserving the name, what minced veal is to a calf.'
That simile has a violence to it that the comic surface barely conceals.
These people are not merely fraudulent — they have dismembered what small dignity they possessed and served it back as something else.
Edmund is right, and I think the legal historian in me wants to press on one particular category — the suicide threateners.
Those beggars who will 'make an end of themselves at a quarter to one P.M. on Tuesday' unless a postal order arrives — that is grimly funny, but it is not invented.
The threat of self-destruction as a form of moral extortion was a documented social phenomenon — Dickens would have known it from newspapers, from charitable society reports.
And this is what makes the Betty Higden passages so devastating by contrast.
Because Betty Higden is also a person who chooses death — but her choice comes from a completely different moral place.
She is fleeing the workhouse — the shame of institutional charity — with every last breath she has.
And Dickens does something extraordinary — he gives the river a voice.
The Thames speaks to her and says,
'I am the Relieving Officer appointed by eternal ordinance to do my work; I am not held in estimation according as I shirk it.'
The Relieving Officer was the official who assessed paupers for workhouse admission — the most dreaded functionary in Victorian poor relief.
Dickens hands that title to the river — to death — and the indictment of the actual Poor Law system could not be more complete.
When I read that passage aloud — and I have, many times — the hardest thing to get right is the tenderness.
Because the prose is genuinely beautiful before the horror sets in — 'the young river, dimpled like a young child, playfully gliding away among the trees.'
That idyllic image is doing deliberate work — it's setting up the contrast with the voice that follows.
And then the river says, and this is the line that stops me every time,
'My breast is softer than the pauper-nurse's; death in my arms is peacefuller than among the pauper-wards.'
'Peacefuller' — that's not a word, grammatically — and it doesn't matter, because it is exactly right emotionally.
Dickens breaks grammar because the grammar of the system has already broken Betty Higden.
Oliver puts his finger on something I find myself returning to — the question of what kind of writer Dickens is when he is at his best.
There are readers — and I confess I have known some of them at Oxford — who regard the Betty Higden sections as sentimental.
I think they are profoundly wrong — but I understand the objection, because Dickens is operating at the edge of what sentiment can bear.
What saves him, every time, is the presence of moral seriousness beneath the pathos.
And nowhere is that more apparent than in this passage about the Boffins — this extraordinary declaration about the nature of good and evil.
Dickens writes, of these two unpolished, uneducated people,
'For, Evil often stops short at itself and dies with the doer of it; but Good, never.'
That is not sentimentality — that is a theological proposition delivered with the confidence of a man who has thought about it for a very long time.
I want to press on that, because the Boffins are also the pivot point of the novel's most troubling question about inherited wealth.
Consider what Wegg reveals about old Harmon's will — the document that started everything.
Wegg reads it aloud, and it says,

'Inasmuch as he has never made friends, and has ever had a rebellious family, he, John Harmon, gives to Nicodemus Boffin the Little Mound, which is quite enough for him, and gives the whole rest and residue of his property to the Crown.'
'Quite enough for him' — that contemptuous parenthesis tells you everything about old Harmon's character.
A man who has wrung labour from others for minimum wages, and whose final act is to decide, from the grave, what is and is not enough.
The dust heap is not morally neutral — it comes soaked in the treatment of people like Boffin and his wife.
And yet — and this is what I love about the novel — Boffin survives it.
Or rather, something in the Boffins resists the corruption that the money is supposed to bring.
Dickens tells us that even the hard, wretched old Harmon, in his lifetime, 'had never been so warped but that it knew their moral straightness and respected it.'
Even the villain cannot quite extinguish what is good in them.
Edmund's quote does the theological work — Good, never — but this detail does the novelistic work.
It shows us the principle in action, in a specific human relationship, before Dickens ever announces it as a law.
That tension — between the corrupting force of money and the stubborn persistence of goodness — is at the heart of everything we'll be exploring today.
The Dust Heaps generate wealth, spectacle, satire, and pathos in equal measure — and Dickens refuses to let any single one of those registers dominate.
We'll return after a short break to follow the money further — and to ask what the novel ultimately believes about whether it can be redeemed.

segments.title: Harmon's Masquerade: Plot, Identity, and Deception

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the series working its way through every dark corner of Dickens's last completed novel.
I'm joined today by three extraordinary readers, each of whom brings something quite different to the table.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don whose life's work has been the moral imagination of the Victorian novel.
He reads character before he reads society, and his patience with a text is extraordinary.
Professor James Blackstone brings the legal and social historian's eye — what the institutions actually were, what the law actually did, and what it meant to be powerless inside that machinery.
And Oliver Trevelyan has read more classic novels aloud than perhaps any living person, and he hears this prose the way a musician hears a score.

Today we are deep inside the novel's architecture of disguise and deception — John Harmon's assumed identity, the river's harvest of the dead, and what the narrative does with money, murder, and misdirection.
Edmund, let's begin at the river — the very opening of the novel, where Gaffer Hexam brings something up from the water.
What strikes me first about that opening passage is its extraordinary compression of moral information.
In the space of a single sentence, Dickens tells us everything we need to know about Gaffer's relationship to the dead — and to money.
The prose performs the ritual itself, with that ruthless tripling:
'He chinked it once, and he blew upon it once, and he spat upon it once,—for luck, he hoarsely said—before he put it in his pocket.'
The chiasmus of gesture — coin handled as a lucky charm — is almost liturgical.
Gaffer does not pocket the money and move on. He consecrates it.
This is the novel's first moral statement: the dead are currency, and currency corrupts absolutely.
Edmund is entirely right about the tripling — it's written for the voice, not the page.
When I've read that passage aloud, I find myself slowing involuntarily at 'hoarsely said' — the adverb is doing enormous work.
Gaffer's voice is the river itself: wet, cold, and matter-of-fact about death.
And then there's the washing of the arms, which comes just before — 'his arms were wet and dirty, and he washed them over the side.'
He washes his hands before pocketing the money. That's not hygiene — that's a grotesque parody of absolution.
And it's worth noting that the money he pockets was found on a drowned man — which raises an immediate legal question.
Under Victorian law, property found on a body did not simply belong to the finder. There were complex obligations around reporting to the coroner.
Gaffer's little ritual of luck is also, in plain legal terms, theft from the dead.
The novel opens, in other words, with a crime — and the crime is unremarkable to the man committing it.
That ordinariness is the sharpest detail of all.
And of course that body in the river is entangled with the Harmon murder — the crime that drives the entire plot.
James, Riderhood's accusation against Gaffer — that comes like a thunderclap in the early chapters. What do you make of its legal staging?
Riderhood's deposition is a masterpiece of institutional mimicry.
He uses the formal language of legal testimony — 'I give information,' 'the hand that done that deed' — but the voice underneath is the Thames mud.
Here is the passage, exactly as it stands:

'I give information that the man that done the Harmon Murder is Gaffer Hexam, the man that found the body. The hand of Jesse Hexam, commonly called Gaffer on the river and along shore, is the hand that done that deed. His hand and no other.'
That final triplet — 'his hand and no other' — is not legal language at all. It is the language of the Old Testament.
Dickens has Riderhood adopt the gravity of scripture to give weight to what is almost certainly a false accusation driven by self-interest.
The irony is structural: the grander the language, the more we should suspect the speaker.
James is quite right about the scriptural cadence, and I think it points to something deeper.
Dickens is showing us how easily the forms of moral seriousness can be borrowed by the morally disreputable.
Riderhood drapes himself in ceremony — he even makes a show of examining the drowned cap, turning it 'over and under' — to perform credibility.
It is the same instinct as Gaffer's ritual with the coin — a kind of superstitious legitimation of what is, at bottom, predatory behaviour.
The river world, in this novel, has its own liturgy — and it is entirely in the service of self.
And the cap — the drowned cap — is wonderful as a piece of theatre.
He brushes it 'the wrong way with his sleeve' — and then that wonderfully deadpan parenthesis: 'if it had a right way.'
That is a joke, but it is a joke about a drowned man's hat. Dickens holds both registers simultaneously without flinching.
The comic and the sinister live on exactly the same street in this novel — often in the same sentence.
The identity at the centre of all this — Harmon's disguise, his assumed death — depends on people like the Boffins, who knew him as a boy and chose to protect him.
Oliver, the Boffin passage — Boffin describing the old man's cruelty to the boy — is almost unbearably vivid. What do you hear in it?
The Boffin passage is one of the great set pieces in the novel for a single performer.
It is Boffin speaking to Lightwood, but he is also performing the memory — re-living it as he tells it.
Listen to the architecture of this:

'I have seen him, after Mrs Boffin has given him her mind respecting the claims of the nat'ral affections, catch off Mrs Boffin's bonnet — she wore, in general, a black straw, perched as a matter of convenience on the top of her head — and send it spinning across the yard.'
And then the terrible conclusion: 'received flush on the temple. Which dropped her, Mr Lightwood. Dropped her.'
That repetition — 'dropped her, dropped her' — is not melodrama. It is shock.
Boffin can't quite get past the image, so he says it twice. And neither can we.
The bonnet — the black straw, perched 'as a matter of convenience' — is doing the most delicate work in that passage.
The parenthetical description is affectionate, almost comic — it dignifies Mrs Boffin with a particular, loveable humanity before the blow falls.
Dickens does not give us a generic victim. He gives us a woman whose hat sits on her head in a specific, familiar way.
That is the technique of a novelist in complete command of his material — the detail that makes violence real, not theatrical.
There is also a serious point about power embedded in that scene.
Old Harmon has absolute economic authority over the Boffins. They are his dependants. And yet they defy him — 'times out of number,' as Boffin says.
Boffin says: 'me and Mrs Boffin have stood out against the old man times out of number, till he has called us every name he could lay his tongue to.'
That is a portrait of moral courage in the least glamorous possible register.
The Boffins are not heroes in any grand sense. But they are consistently, stubbornly decent — and the novel knows exactly how rare that is.
Before we close, I want to bring in one more passage — Edmund, the train crossing the river.
It sits at some distance from the Harmon plot, and yet it feels like a key to something in the novel's deeper machinery.
The passage is, on its surface, a description of a railway journey through London.
But Dickens elevates it into something very close to cosmological statement.
The prose reaches its full power at the crossing of the river — let me give you the full weight of it:

'the train rattled among the house-tops, and among the ragged sides of houses torn down to make way for it, and over the swarming streets, and under the fruitful earth, until it shot across the river: bursting over the quiet surface like a bomb-shell, and gone again as if it had exploded in the rush of smoke and steam and glare.'
That contrast — the 'quiet surface' of the river and the bomb-shell violence of the train — is not accidental.
The river in this novel is the medium of death, of slow time, of the recovered body. The train is industrial modernity — impatient, contemptuous of the natural world.
And then the final clause draws them together under the same jurisdiction: Father Time, who is indifferent to all of it.
'Going straight to its end, as Father Time goes to his' — that is a sentence that arrives like a closing door.
And there is something almost unbearable in the following lines — 'To whom it is no matter what living waters run high or low.'

'To whom it is no matter what living waters run high or low, reflect the heavenly lights and darknesses, produce their little growth of weeds and flowers... for their course has one sure termination.'
'Their little growth of weeds and flowers' — that is every human life in four words.
When Dickens is at his best, you can hear the whole novel in a single clause. This is that.
What strikes me is that the train is described as 'spurning the watery turnings and doublings with ineffable contempt.'
The word 'contempt' is remarkable. It is usually a human attitude — a social and moral judgment.
To apply it to a train crossing a river is to imply that industrial modernity does not merely move through the landscape — it judges it, dismisses it.
And the novel, throughout, is about what gets left behind when modernity arrives in that contemptuous rush.
That image — the bomb-shell across the quiet water, and Father Time unmoved by all of it — feels like as good a place as any to pause in our reading of this extraordinary novel.
My thanks to Sir Edmund Leigh, Professor James Blackstone, and Oliver Trevelyan.
We'll continue our close reading of Our Mutual Friend in the next episode — further into the labyrinth of money, disguise, and the dark, patient river.

segments.title: Comic Relief and the Art of Dickensian Wit

utterances.text: Welcome back to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.
We've been exploring the novel's darker currents — the river, the dust, the predatory world of inheritance.
But Dickens is also, before anything else, a comedian of genius.
This segment is devoted to the wit: the satire, the grotesques, the perfectly timed comic strokes that run through this novel like a bright thread.
And there is no one better placed to lead us through this territory than Oliver Trevelyan — actor, writer, and the man who has read more Dickens aloud than perhaps anyone living.
I'm enormously grateful for that introduction, and I want to start with possibly the most famous five words in this entire novel.
Betty Higden is explaining to Mrs Boffin that young Sloppy has a particular gift.
"He do the Police in different voices."
Nine words, actually — I miscounted — but every single one of them is doing work.
The grammar is gloriously wrong, the image is precise and strange, and there's a whole portrait of a boy and an old woman in it.
Sloppy reads the police reports in different voices — that's his art, his compensation for everything life has denied him.
It is, I think, a line which reveals something essential about Dickens's relationship with his characters.
He does not condescend to Betty Higden by correcting her grammar.
He gives her the dignity of her own idiom, and in doing so he gives Sloppy the dignity of genuine achievement.
The full passage is tender in precisely that way: she reads her Bible and most print, she cannot manage handwriting, and yet she loves a newspaper.
That is characterisation of the highest moral order — you see the whole person.
It's also worth noting what the newspapers meant to people like Betty Higden.
The police columns were genuinely popular reading — they were the drama of the streets, accessible even to the barely literate when read aloud by someone like Sloppy.
So when Dickens gives us that line, he is also describing a real social practice — communal reading, oral culture surviving alongside print culture.
The comedy and the social document are completely inseparable.
And that inseparability is what makes the comic writing in this novel so sustainable — it never feels like a relief from the serious matter, it feels like another way into it.
Take Mrs Sprodgkin — a character most people forget but who is devastatingly observed.
The narrator tells us she had, and I want to read this carefully,
"an infection of absurdity about her, that communicated itself to everything with which, and everybody with whom, she came in contact."
An infection of absurdity — that is a phrase worth stopping for.
And then the specifics: she conspicuously wept at everything, however cheering, said by the Reverend Frank in his public ministry.
However cheering! — the comedy is entirely in those two words.
What I find admirable — and here I may be swimming against the critical current — is that Dickens does not despise Mrs Sprodgkin.
The Milveys bear with her with what the narrator calls exemplary sweetness and good-humour.
They make the best of her, as they did of all their troubles.
There is a moral seriousness behind the satire — the comedy earns its keep because it is in service of a portrait of genuine Christian charity.
And the religious affectation Dickens is satirising here is a very particular Victorian phenomenon.
The way she discharges the Morning and Evening Service — as if lodging a complaint before a magistrate — that is a precise comic diagnosis of performative piety.
She has converted religion into grievance, and Dickens understands that this is both ridiculous and, in some way, pitiable.
Now let me bring us to a very different kind of comic moment — one that is pure performance.
The Deputy Lock, pocketing Betty Higden's coins one by one while declaring his own virtue.

"I'm a man as earns his living by the sweat of his brow" — and here he draws his sleeve across his forehead, as if this particular portion of his humble gains were the result of sheer hard labour and virtuous industry.
The gesture is everything — wiping the sweat that is absolutely not there.
It is theatrical hypocrisy performed with total conviction, and Dickens directs it with the economy of a stage direction.
The corruption of minor officials is something Dickens returns to repeatedly, and it is rooted in reality.
Lock-keepers, parish overseers, clerks — they occupied positions of tiny power over people who had no recourse, and they knew it.
Betty Higden is old, on foot, alone — and this man pockets her money and tells her to go where she likes.
The comedy barely conceals something genuinely ugly.
Which is precisely why the comedy is not decoration but substance.
Johnson observed that no man who ever smiled at Falstaff's cowardice could remain entirely comfortable — comedy implicates its audience.
Here, Dickens makes the Deputy Lock laughable so that we do not look away from him.
And then, as a perfect counterpoint, there's the moment with the Secretary and Silas Wegg — which is the opposite of slow comic insinuation.
It is pure, sudden, magnificent threat.
The Secretary has just thrown something out, and he turns to Wegg and says,
"Be careful what insolent liberties you take in that gentleman's presence, or I will throw you after it."
There is no elaboration, no qualifying clause — just that.
The comedy comes from the absolute economy of it, and from the fact that you believe he means it completely.
There is a tradition — I believe Burke touches on it — of the sublime in miniature: the concentrated utterance that achieves more than the elaborated speech.
That line has the quality of an epigram rather than a threat — perfectly weighted, perfectly timed.
What strikes me about all four of these moments is how they all circle around questions of power — who has it, who is pretending to have it, who is utterly without it.
Sloppy reads the Police in different voices for an old woman who cannot manage handwriting — that is power of a very modest and tender kind.
The Deputy Lock wields petty institutional power with maximum self-congratulation.
Mrs Sprodgkin has found a way to make her powerlessness felt as imposition on others.
And the Secretary's line is power exercised with absolute directness, in defence of a good man.
That is beautifully put, and it explains why the comedy never exhausts itself — it is always in conversation with something that matters.
Dickens is the most serious of all comic novelists, which is perhaps why he remains the most entertaining.
Serious, entertaining, and inexhaustible — that seems a fine note on which to pause.
After the break, we'll turn to the novel's treatment of money — its origins, its corruptions, and what it does to the people who inherit it.
Welcome back to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.
We've been tracing the great moral arc of Dickens's final completed novel — and in this segment, we turn to the question of transformation itself.
Who changes, who refuses to, and what does the novel make of the difference?
With me today, as ever, are three distinguished voices — each bringing a quite different lens to the text.
Sir Edmund Leigh, retired Oxford don and the conscience of what I might call the close moral reading — the belief that character, not system, is the engine of great fiction.
Professor James Blackstone, legal and social historian, who reminds us that every fictional institution stands on a real one — and that the real ones had teeth.

And Oliver Trevelyan — actor, writer, and narrator of more classic novels than any human being should reasonably have attempted — who reads Dickens above all as performance, as voice, as the pleasure of language on the ear.
Edmund, I'd like to start with you — because this segment brings together passages from quite different registers of the novel, and you're rather beautifully placed across all of them.
Thank you — and I think the word 'transformation' is precisely the right one, though one must be careful not to sentimentalise it.
Dickens is not optimistic in any easy sense.
He gives us characters who genuinely change — and he gives us, alongside them, characters who are constitutionally incapable of it.
Silas Wegg is the great exemplar of the second category.
There is a passage in which Wegg lays out his scheme with, one must say, a kind of monstrous administrative precision.

He considers it plain that such price was stateable in a single expressive word, and that the word was, 'Halves!' — and that Boffin should be kept in a state of abject moral bondage and slavery until the time when they should see fit to permit him to purchase his freedom at the price of half his possessions.
'Abject moral bondage and slavery.' That is Wegg's own language — his language for what he intends to inflict on another human being.
Dickens gives the villainy its own rhetoric — and it is the rhetoric of property and contract.
That point about the rhetoric of contract is worth dwelling on.
Wegg doesn't just want money — he wants a legal-sounding framework for extortion.
The 'comrade, brother, and partner' formula — repeated with almost parliamentary insistence — is a grotesque parody of the partnership deed.
The real Chancery and the real property law of the 1860s were instruments of exactly this kind of slow, grinding dispossession — just with better vocabulary.
Dickens understood — perhaps better than any novelist before or since — that legalistic language is how respectable people bully those beneath them.
Wegg is not an anomaly; he is a low mirror held up to the high world of Veneering and Podsnap.
And yet — I want to say something in defence of Wegg's entertainment value, because I think it matters to the novel's design.
Dickens gives him that wonderful plan — lie in wait, let Boffin pay for the digging, then swoop — which is so gloriously, impractically overengineered.

And the conditional clause! — 'if the minion should return in his late sneaking manner' — the whole thing is pitched at exactly the wrong level of formality for a man with a wooden leg conspiring in a garden bower.
But then comes the resolution — and it is, I have to say, one of the great comic coups in all of Dickens.
Somebody else had come in quietly by the folding-doors.
Turning his head, Wegg beheld his persecutor, the ever-wakeful dustman, accoutred with fantail hat and velveteen smalls complete.
Who, untying his tied-up broken head, revealed a head that was whole, and a face that was Sloppy's.
'A face that was Sloppy's.' The whole edifice of Wegg's scheming undone by that glorious idiot in a fantail hat.
It is funny — I grant you it is very funny.
But the comedy is not merely decorative.
Sloppy — who was himself an object of charity, a child of the dust heaps — is the instrument by which the universe corrects Wegg's grotesque ambition.
Providence has a sense of humour in this novel.
And that moral geometry — the low brought low by the lower, so that the genuinely good may rise — is everywhere in the book.
It is, I think, central to understanding what Dickens means by redemption — which brings me to Bella Wilfer and that extraordinary supper passage.

The narrator describes it as like the supper provided for the three nursery hobgoblins at their house in the forest, without their thunderous low growlings of the alarming discovery, 'Somebody's been drinking my milk!'
It was a delicious repast; by far the most delicious that Bella, or John Rokesmith, or even R. Wilfer had ever made.
The fairy tale reference is not whimsy — it is Dickens signalling that these three have entered, at last, the realm of happiness that the novel's opening world of dust and money denied them.
The detail of the iron safe in the corner is what gets me every time.
'The two brass knobs of the iron safe of Chicksey, Veneering, and Stobbles staring from a corner, like the eyes of some dull dragon' — they eat their fairy tale feast in the counting house.
The happiness is not purchased by escaping the commercial world — it is wrested from within it.
That is rather precise social observation on Dickens's part, actually.
The lower middle class of the 1860s could not simply opt out of the economy — love had to coexist with the brass knobs.
R. Wilfer — even in a moment of pure tenderness, Dickens cannot resist his own joke.
The father who exists in a kind of permanent, cheerful subordination — his initial used in place of a name, as if the name were still too grand for him.
And yet he is included — 'the most delicious that Bella, or John Rokesmith, or even R. Wilfer had ever made' — that 'even' doing a great deal of delicate emotional work.
The 'even' tells you that R. Wilfer's life has not, until now, contained very many delicious repasts — and the sentence wraps him in without making a speech about it.
That is Dickens the performer — the sentiment is there, but the timing prevents it from becoming sticky.
Oliver's instinct there connects directly to what I find most compelling in the Eugene Wrayburn material.
Eugene is the character in the novel who most clearly articulates his own incapacity for transformation — and does so with a kind of elegant, rueful precision.
Lightwood begins to urge him to look to the future — and there is a passage where Eugene simply catches the phrase and holds it.
'Look on to the end—' Lightwood was beginning to remonstrate, when he caught at the words.
And what makes the moment devastating is what the narrator adds: that Eugene said it, quote, 'with a perplexed and inquisitive face, as if he actually did not know what to make of himself.'
He is not performing languid indifference — he genuinely cannot locate himself in a future.
That self-knowledge without self-command is one of Dickens's most original contributions to the psychology of character.
It's worth noting the class context there — Eugene's paralysis is the paralysis of a man trained for nothing, because men of his class were not supposed to need training.
The Bar was the respectable holding pattern for clever young men who hadn't an estate to manage.
Eugene knows he's in the holding pattern — that's precisely the self-knowledge Edmund identifies — but the system gave him no mechanism for breaking out of it.
It takes near-death and a woman of quite extraordinary moral force to do what the institution of the Bar could not.
And the voice captures it — 'That's exactly what I am incapable of doing' — said gaily, the narrator tells us, but with a perplexed face.
That simultaneous tone — the lightness on the lips, the bewilderment in the eyes — is almost impossible to write, and Dickens does it in ten words.
When you read it aloud, you have to hold both things at once — and the audience feels the crack in the comedy before they can name it.
And that crack in the comedy is, in a sense, where the whole novel lives — between what is said gaily and what is meant gravely.
We've moved today from Wegg's monstrous legalism to a fairy tale supper in a counting house, from Eugene's exquisite self-paralysis to Sloppy's face beneath the bandage.
What unites them, I think, is Dickens's insistence that transformation is real — earned, not given — and that comedy and sorrow are not separate instruments but a single chord.
My thanks to Sir Edmund Leigh, Professor James Blackstone, and Oliver Trevelyan.
We'll continue our exploration of Our Mutual Friend in the next segment.
We've been moving through this novel's great preoccupations all episode — money, identity, the river, the dead.
And I think it's time to ask what the novel finally says about all of it — whether it offers consolation, or merely witness.
Edmund, I want to start with you — because you've been the conscience of this conversation — on the question of virtue and wealth.
There's a passage early in the novel — when the narrator reflects on old John Harmon and the Boffins — that I find quietly devastating.
It concerns what misanthropy actually perceives, when it's honest with itself.
The narrator tells us that the old man raged at them, reviled them — and yet, the prose says something precise and startling.
"he had perceived the powerlessness of all his wealth to buy them if he had addressed himself to the attempt."
Powerlessness. Of all his wealth.
The novel's great subject announced in a subordinate clause — that there exists a human integrity which money cannot purchase.
Dickens is not, here, writing a programme. He is recording a truth about character — and the old miser knows it, even as he denies it.
What strikes me about that passage is the legal instrument it leads to — the will.
The old man writes their names down. That is his only act of acknowledged trust — performed in private, after death, with no witness.
In the Victorian legal world, a testamentary bequest of that kind was enormously consequential — and enormously exposable to contest.
The entire plot turns on it. Fortunes, disguises, the river itself — all set in motion by one dead man's grudging admission that two people were honest.
Dickens understood that the law could be the instrument of posthumous tyranny just as much as posthumous grace.
And against all that legal machinery and moral gravity, Dickens gives us one of the most purely joyful moments in the whole book.
Rokesmith — or rather, John Harmon finally unmasked — bursting into the counting-house and catching Bella in his arms.
The prose practically trips over itself with delight. Listen to this:
"My dear, dear girl; my gallant, generous, disinterested, courageous, noble girl!"
Five adjectives. Five. And he's not done.
Then: "Bella, after hanging her head for a moment, lifted it up and laid it on his breast, as if that were her head's chosen and lasting resting-place."
Chosen and lasting resting-place. The whole novel in a phrase — things finding where they belong, after a long and complicated journey.
It's a wonderfully comic scene, yes — but I'd argue it's also the novel's moral argument made flesh.
Bella has passed through her testing. She has chosen love over wealth — not once, but repeatedly, when it cost her something.
And the reward — if we call it that — is not wealth restored but selfhood recovered. Hers, and his.
But Dickens won't let us rest in that warmth entirely. Almost simultaneously, the novel is moving toward its darkest passage.
Bradley Headstone following Eugene Wrayburn along the river — that Gothic pursuit — is happening in the same stretch of the novel.
The landscape carries it. The prose is quite extraordinary — the bargeman skulking on the opposite bank, the sun going down, the landscape dyed red.
"And then the red had the appearance of fading out of it and mounting up to Heaven, as we say that blood, guiltily shed, does."
Blood, guiltily shed. That phrase is doing something the law cannot — it is describing a moral stain before the act has even occurred.
When I read that passage aloud — and I have, more than once — the rhythm does half the work.
It rises. The red fades out of the landscape and mounts — that verb, mounts — up to Heaven.
And then 'as we say' — that quiet aside, the narrator stepping in, reminding us this is a shared knowledge, a folk truth about guilt.
Dickens is the greatest writer of dread in English prose. Not horror — dread. The slow certainty that something terrible is coming.
And the river holds all of it — the comedy and the dread, the lovers and the murderer, the drowned man who refused to stay dead.
That, I think, is the structural genius of the novel. Not the plot's ingenuity, though that is considerable.
But the river as the one image capacious enough to contain everything the novel needs to say about life and death and what we owe one another.
That feels like exactly the right place to end — with the river, doing what only great art can: holding opposites in suspension.
My thanks to Edmund Leigh, James Blackstone, and Oliver Trevelyan — for a conversation that has done this novel considerable justice.
Our Mutual Friend is a novel that rewards exactly this kind of attention — it gives back more than you bring to it.
Until next time, this has been Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.

‘I examined the newspapers every day for tidings that I was missing, but
      saw none. Going out that night to walk (for I kept retired while it was
      light), I found a crowd assembled round a placard posted at Whitehall. It
      described myself, John Harmon, as found dead and mutilated in the river
      under circumstances of strong suspicion, described my dress, described the
      papers in my pockets, and stated where I was lying for recognition. In a
      wild incautious way I hurried there, and there—with the horror of
      the death I had escaped, before my eyes in its most appalling shape, added
      to the inconceivable horror tormenting me at that time when the poisonous
      stuff was strongest on me—I perceived that Radfoot had been murdered
      by some unknown hands for the money for which he would have murdered me,
      and that probably we had both been shot into the river from the same dark
      place into the same dark tide, when the stream ran deep and strong.
c30:p27.summary: John Harmon recounts finding the placard announcing the discovery of his own body in the river, then learning that it was actually Radfoot's corpse dressed in John's clothes, murdered for money.

c8:p43.text:
‘The last time me and Mrs Boffin saw the poor boy,’ said Mr Boffin,
      warming (as fat usually does) with a tendency to melt, ‘he was a child of
      seven year old. For when he came back to make intercession for his sister,
      me and Mrs Boffin were away overlooking a country contract which was to be
      sifted before carted, and he was come and gone in a single hour. I say he
      was a child of seven year old. He was going away, all alone and forlorn,
      to that foreign school, and he come into our place, situate up the yard of
      the present Bower, to have a warm at our fire. There was his little scanty
      travelling clothes upon him. There was his little scanty box outside in
      the shivering wind, which I was going to carry for him down to the
      steamboat, as the old man wouldn’t hear of allowing a sixpence
      coach-money. Mrs Boffin, then quite a young woman and pictur of a
      full-blown rose, stands him by her, kneels down at the fire, warms her two
      open hands, and falls to rubbing his cheeks; but seeing the tears come
      into the child’s eyes, the tears come fast into her own, and she holds him
      round the neck, like as if she was protecting him, and cries to me, “I’d
      give the wide wide world, I would, to run away with him!” I don’t say but
      what it cut me, and but what it at the same time heightened my feelings of
      admiration for Mrs Boffin. The poor child clings to her for awhile, as she
      clings to him, and then, when the old man calls, he says “I must go! God
      bless you!” and for a moment rests his heart against her bosom, and looks
      up at both of us, as if it was in pain—in agony. Such a look! I went
      aboard with him (I gave him first what little treat I thought he’d like),
      and I left him when he had fallen asleep in his berth, and I came back to
      Mrs Boffin. But tell her what I would of how I had left him, it all went
      for nothing, for, according to her thoughts, he never changed that look
      that he had looked up at us two. But it did one piece of good. Mrs Boffin
      and me had no child of our own, and had sometimes wished that how we had
      one. But not now. “We might both of us die,” says Mrs Boffin, “and other
      eyes might see that lonely look in our child.” So of a night, when it was
      very cold, or when the wind roared, or the rain dripped heavy, she would
      wake sobbing, and call out in a fluster, “Don’t you see the poor child’s
      face? O shelter the poor child!”—till in course of years it gently
      wore out, as many things do.’
c8:p43.summary: Boffin recounts the last time he and Mrs Boffin saw young John Harmon, a seven-year-old being sent to a foreign school, including the poignant moment when Mrs Boffin wept while warming the boy by the fire and embraced him protectively, expressing a desire to save him—a memory that haunted her for years.

‘I have checked the calculation often, and it must have been two nights
      that I lay recovering in that public-house. Let me see. Yes. I am sure it
      was while I lay in that bed there, that the thought entered my head of

      dread of our being forced on one another, and perpetuating the fate that

      should lead to nothing but evil—was strong upon the moral timidity

‘However, a sociable word or two on these mistakes became an easy
      introduction between us, and the weather was hot, and he helped me to a
      cool cabin on deck alongside his own, and his first school had been at
      Brussels as mine had been, and he had learnt French as I had learnt it,
      and he had a little history of himself to relate—God only knows how
      much of it true, and how much of it false—that had its likeness to
      mine. I had been a seaman too. So we got to be confidential together, and
      the more easily yet, because he and every one on board had known by
      general rumour what I was making the voyage to England for. By such
      degrees and means, he came to the knowledge of my uneasiness of mind, and
      of its setting at that time in the direction of desiring to see and form
      some judgment of my allotted wife, before she could possibly know me for
      myself; also to try Mrs Boffin and give her a glad surprise. So the plot
      was made out of our getting common sailors’ dresses (as he was able to
      guide me about London), and throwing ourselves in Bella Wilfer’s
      neighbourhood, and trying to put ourselves in her way, and doing whatever
      chance might favour on the spot, and seeing what came of it. If nothing
      came of it, I should be no worse off, and there would merely be a short
      delay in my presenting myself to Lightwood. I have all these facts right?
      Yes. They are all accurately right.

‘And therefore—and therefore,’ the cherub went on in a glowing
      voice, as Bella’s hand stole gradually up his waistcoat to his neck, ‘this
      mercenary young person distantly related to myself, refused the price,
      took off the splendid fashions that were part of it, put on the
      comparatively poor dress that I had last given her, and trusting to my

c49:p74.best_quote: The mercenary young person distantly related to myself, did well! The mercenary young person distantly related to myself, did not trust to me in vain! I admire this mercenary young person distantly related to myself, more in this dress than if she had come to me in China silks, Cashmere shawls, and Golconda diamonds. I love this young person dearly. I say to the man of this young person's heart, out of my heart and with all of it, "My blessing on this engagement betwixt you, and she brings you a good fortune when she brings you the poverty she has accepted for your sake and the honest truth's!"

‘I don’t. And if  they  do, my dear, they ought to learn better,’ said Mr
      Boffin. ‘Patrons and Patronesses, and Vice-Patrons and Vice-Patronesses,
      and Deceased Patrons and Deceased Patronesses, and Ex-Vice-Patrons and
      Ex-Vice-Patronesses, what does it all mean in the books of the Charities
      that come pouring in on Rokesmith as he sits among ’em pretty well up to
      his neck! If Mr Tom Noakes gives his five shillings ain’t he a Patron, and
      if Mrs Jack Styles gives her five shillings ain’t she a Patroness? What
      the deuce is it all about? If it ain’t stark staring impudence, what do
      you call it?’

c17:p4.text:
But no one knows so well as the Secretary, who opens and reads the
      letters, what a set is made at the man marked by a stroke of notoriety. Oh
      the varieties of dust for ocular use, offered in exchange for the gold
      dust of the Golden Dustman! Fifty-seven churches to be erected with
      half-crowns, forty-two parsonage houses to be repaired with shillings,
      seven-and-twenty organs to be built with halfpence, twelve hundred
      children to be brought up on postage stamps. Not that a half-crown,
      shilling, halfpenny, or postage stamp, would be particularly acceptable
      from Mr Boffin, but that it is so obvious he is the man to make up the
      deficiency. And then the charities, my Christian brother! And mostly in
      difficulties, yet mostly lavish, too, in the expensive articles of print
      and paper. Large fat private double letter, sealed with ducal coronet.
      ‘Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire. My Dear Sir,—Having consented to preside
      at the forthcoming Annual Dinner of the Family Party Fund, and feeling
      deeply impressed with the immense usefulness of that noble Institution and
      the great importance of its being supported by a List of Stewards that
      shall prove to the public the interest taken in it by popular and
      distinguished men, I have undertaken to ask you to become a Steward on
      that occasion. Soliciting your favourable reply before the 14th instant, I
      am, My Dear Sir, Your faithful Servant,  Linseed . P.S. The Steward’s fee is
      limited to three Guineas.’ Friendly this, on the part of the Duke of
      Linseed (and thoughtful in the postscript), only lithographed by the
      hundred and presenting but a pale individuality of an address to Nicodemus
      Boffin, Esquire, in quite another hand. It takes two noble Earls and a
      Viscount, combined, to inform Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, in an equally
      flattering manner, that an estimable lady in the West of England has
      offered to present a purse containing twenty pounds, to the Society for
      Granting Annuities to Unassuming Members of the Middle Classes, if twenty
      individuals will previously present purses of one hundred pounds each. And
      those benevolent noblemen very kindly point out that if Nicodemus Boffin,
      Esquire, should wish to present two or more purses, it will not be
      inconsistent with the design of the estimable lady in the West of England,
      provided each purse be coupled with the name of some member of his
      honoured and respected family.
c17:p4.summary: The Secretary describes the flood of charitable solicitations and scheme proposals that inundate the Boffins, including a satirical example of a duke's letter requesting Boffin become a Steward of a charity for a three-guinea fee.
c17:p4.best_quote: Large fat private double letter, sealed with ducal coronet.

c17:p5.text:
These are the corporate beggars. But there are, besides, the individual
      beggars; and how does the heart of the Secretary fail him when he has to
      cope with  them!  And they must be coped with to some extent, because they
      all enclose documents (they call their scraps documents; but they are, as
      to papers deserving the name, what minced veal is to a calf), the
      non-return of which would be their ruin. That is to say, they are utterly
      ruined now, but they would be more utterly ruined then. Among these
      correspondents are several daughters of general officers, long accustomed
      to every luxury of life (except spelling), who little thought, when their
      gallant fathers waged war in the Peninsula, that they would ever have to
      appeal to those whom Providence, in its inscrutable wisdom, has blessed
      with untold gold, and from among whom they select the name of Nicodemus
      Boffin, Esquire, for a maiden effort in this wise, understanding that he
      has such a heart as never was. The Secretary learns, too, that confidence
      between man and wife would seem to obtain but rarely when virtue is in
      distress, so numerous are the wives who take up their pens to ask Mr
      Boffin for money without the knowledge of their devoted husbands, who
      would never permit it; while, on the other hand, so numerous are the
      husbands who take up their pens to ask Mr Boffin for money without the
      knowledge of their devoted wives, who would instantly go out of their
      senses if they had the least suspicion of the circumstance. There are the
      inspired beggars, too. These were sitting, only yesterday evening, musing
      over a fragment of candle which must soon go out and leave them in the
      dark for the rest of their nights, when surely some Angel whispered the
      name of Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, to their souls, imparting rays of hope,
      nay confidence, to which they had long been strangers! Akin to these are
      the suggestively-befriended beggars. They were partaking of a cold potato
      and water by the flickering and gloomy light of a lucifer-match, in their
      lodgings (rent considerably in arrear, and heartless landlady threatening
      expulsion ‘like a dog’ into the streets), when a gifted friend happening
      to look in, said, ‘Write immediately to Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire,’ and
      would take no denial. There are the nobly independent beggars too. These,
      in the days of their abundance, ever regarded gold as dross, and have not
      yet got over that only impediment in the way of their amassing wealth, but
      they want no dross from Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire; No, Mr Boffin; the
      world may term it pride, paltry pride if you will, but they wouldn’t take
      it if you offered it; a loan, sir—for fourteen weeks to the day,
      interest calculated at the rate of five per cent per annum, to be bestowed
      upon any charitable institution you may name—is all they want of
      you, and if you have the meanness to refuse it, count on being despised by
      these great spirits. There are the beggars of punctual business-habits
      too. These will make an end of themselves at a quarter to one P.M. on
      Tuesday, if no Post-office order is in the interim received from Nicodemus
      Boffin, Esquire; arriving after a quarter to one P.M. on Tuesday, it need
      not be sent, as they will then (having made an exact memorandum of the
      heartless circumstances) be ‘cold in death.’ There are the beggars on
      horseback too, in another sense from the sense of the proverb. These are
      mounted and ready to start on the highway to affluence. The goal is before
      them, the road is in the best condition, their spurs are on, the steed is
      willing, but, at the last moment, for want of some special thing—a
      clock, a violin, an astronomical telescope, an electrifying machine—they
      must dismount for ever, unless they receive its equivalent in money from
      Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire. Less given to detail are the beggars who make
      sporting ventures. These, usually to be addressed in reply under initials
      at a country post-office, inquire in feminine hands, Dare one who cannot
      disclose herself to Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, but whose name might
      startle him were it revealed, solicit the immediate advance of two hundred
      pounds from unexpected riches exercising their noblest privilege in the
      trust of a common humanity?
c17:p5.summary: The Secretary catalogs individual beggars seeking Boffin's charity—daughters of officers, distressed wives and husbands, those claiming divine inspiration, independent beggars offering loans, and those threatening suicide—each category satirically anatomized.
c17:p5.best_quote: they call their scraps documents; but they are, as to papers deserving the name, what minced veal is to a calf

c41:p7.text:
In those pleasant little towns on Thames, you may hear the fall of the
      water over the weirs, or even, in still weather, the rustle of the rushes;
      and from the bridge you may see the young river, dimpled like a young
      child, playfully gliding away among the trees, unpolluted by the
      defilements that lie in wait for it on its course, and as yet out of
      hearing of the deep summons of the sea. It were too much to pretend that
      Betty Higden made out such thoughts; no; but she heard the tender river
      whispering to many like herself, ‘Come to me, come to me! When the cruel
      shame and terror you have so long fled from, most beset you, come to me! I
      am the Relieving Officer appointed by eternal ordinance to do my work; I
      am not held in estimation according as I shirk it. My breast is softer
      than the pauper-nurse’s; death in my arms is peacefuller than among the
      pauper-wards. Come to me!’
c41:p7.summary: Dickens uses vivid description of the river landscape to imagine the Thames itself whispering an invitation to the suffering and desperate—offering death as a kinder relief than institutional charity.

c9:p29.text:
These two ignorant and unpolished people had guided themselves so far on
      in their journey of life, by a religious sense of duty and desire to do
      right. Ten thousand weaknesses and absurdities might have been detected in
      the breasts of both; ten thousand vanities additional, possibly, in the
      breast of the woman. But the hard wrathful and sordid nature that had
      wrung as much work out of them as could be got in their best days, for as
      little money as could be paid to hurry on their worst, had never been so
      warped but that it knew their moral straightness and respected it. In its
      own despite, in a constant conflict with itself and them, it had done so.
      And this is the eternal law. For, Evil often stops short at itself and
      dies with the doer of it; but Good, never.
c9:p29.summary: Dickens reflects that the Boffins, though ignorant and unpolished, have been guided by genuine religious duty and moral righteousness that even hardened souls cannot entirely resist.

‘And speaking of satisfactory,’ pursued Mr Boffin, ‘why, Lord save us!
      when we come to take it to pieces, bit by bit, where’s the
      satisfactoriness of the money as yet? When the old man does right the poor

      lips. Mr Lightwood, I will now name to you, that on behalf of the poor
      dear boy, me and Mrs Boffin have stood out against the old man times out
      of number, till he has called us every name he could lay his tongue to. I
      have seen him, after Mrs Boffin has given him her mind respecting the
      claims of the nat’ral affections, catch off Mrs Boffin’s bonnet (she wore,
      in general, a black straw, perched as a matter of convenience on the top
      of her head), and send it spinning across the yard. I have indeed. And
      once, when he did this in a manner that amounted to personal, I should
      have given him a rattler for himself, if Mrs Boffin hadn’t thrown herself
      betwixt us, and received flush on the temple. Which dropped her, Mr
      Lightwood. Dropped her.’

c61:p86.text:
Then, the train rattled among the house-tops, and among the ragged sides
      of houses torn down to make way for it, and over the swarming streets, and
      under the fruitful earth, until it shot across the river: bursting over
      the quiet surface like a bomb-shell, and gone again as if it had exploded
      in the rush of smoke and steam and glare. A little more, and again it
      roared across the river, a great rocket: spurning the watery turnings and
      doublings with ineffable contempt, and going straight to its end, as
      Father Time goes to his. To whom it is no matter what living waters run
      high or low, reflect the heavenly lights and darknesses, produce their
      little growth of weeds and flowers, turn here, turn there, are noisy or
      still, are troubled or at rest, for their course has one sure termination,
      though their sources and devices are many.

c61:p48.text:
That worthy couple were delayed by a portentous old parishioner of the
      female gender, who was one of the plagues of their lives, and with whom
      they bore with most exemplary sweetness and good-humour, notwithstanding
      her having an infection of absurdity about her, that communicated itself
      to everything with which, and everybody with whom, she came in contact.
      She was a member of the Reverend Frank’s congregation, and made a point of
      distinguishing herself in that body, by conspicuously weeping at
      everything, however cheering, said by the Reverend Frank in his public
      ministration; also by applying to herself the various lamentations of
      David, and complaining in a personally injured manner (much in arrear of
      the clerk and the rest of the respondents) that her enemies were digging
      pit-falls about her, and breaking her with rods of iron. Indeed, this old
      widow discharged herself of that portion of the Morning and Evening
      Service as if she were lodging a complaint on oath and applying for a
      warrant before a magistrate. But this was not her most inconvenient
      characteristic, for that took the form of an impression, usually recurring
      in inclement weather and at about daybreak, that she had something on her
      mind and stood in immediate need of the Reverend Frank to come and take it
      off. Many a time had that kind creature got up, and gone out to Mrs
      Sprodgkin (such was the disciple’s name), suppressing a strong sense of
      her comicality by his strong sense of duty, and perfectly knowing that
      nothing but a cold would come of it. However, beyond themselves, the
      Reverend Frank Milvey and Mrs Milvey seldom hinted that Mrs Sprodgkin was
      hardly worth the trouble she gave; but both made the best of her, as they
      did of all their troubles.

c40:p72.text:
On this head, Silas Wegg had much to say. Silas had to say That, he would
      beg to remind his comrade, brother, and partner, of the impressive
      passages they had read that evening; of the evident parallel in Mr
      Boffin’s mind between them and the late owner of the Bower, and the
      present circumstances of the Bower; of the bottle; and of the box. That,
      the fortunes of his brother and comrade, and of himself were evidently
      made, inasmuch as they had but to put their price upon this document, and
      get that price from the minion of fortune and the worm of the hour: who
      now appeared to be less of a minion and more of a worm than had been
      previously supposed. That, he considered it plain that such price was
      stateable in a single expressive word, and that the word was, ‘Halves!’
      That, the question then arose when ‘Halves!’ should be called. That, here
      he had a plan of action to recommend, with a conditional clause. That, the
      plan of action was that they should lie by with patience; that, they
      should allow the Mounds to be gradually levelled and cleared away, while
      retaining to themselves their present opportunity of watching the process—which
      would be, he conceived, to put the trouble and cost of daily digging and
      delving upon somebody else, while they might nightly turn such complete
      disturbance of the dust to the account of their own private investigations—and
      that, when the Mounds were gone, and they had worked those chances for
      their own joint benefit solely, they should then, and not before, explode
      on the minion and worm. But here came the conditional clause, and to this
      he entreated the special attention of his comrade, brother, and partner.
      It was not to be borne that the minion and worm should carry off any of
      that property which was now to be regarded as their own property. When he,
      Mr Wegg, had seen the minion surreptitiously making off with that bottle,
      and its precious contents unknown, he had looked upon him in the light of
      a mere robber, and, as such, would have despoiled him of his ill-gotten
      gain, but for the judicious interference of his comrade, brother, and
      partner. Therefore, the conditional clause he proposed was, that, if the
      minion should return in his late sneaking manner, and if, being closely
      watched, he should be found to possess himself of anything, no matter
      what, the sharp sword impending over his head should be instantly shown
      him, he should be strictly examined as to what he knew or suspected,
      should be severely handled by them his masters, and should be kept in a
      state of abject moral bondage and slavery until the time when they should
      see fit to permit him to purchase his freedom at the price of half his
      possessions. If, said Mr Wegg by way of peroration, he had erred in saying
      only ‘Halves!’ he trusted to his comrade, brother, and partner not to
      hesitate to set him right, and to reprove his weakness. It might be more
      according to the rights of things, to say Two-thirds; it might be more
      according to the rights of things, to say Three-fourths. On those points
      he was ever open to correction.

If Boffin is caught secretly removing anything, they will interrogate and enslave him morally until he pays for his freedom.

Through his most inveterate purposes, the dead Jailer of Harmony Jail had
      known these two faithful servants to be honest and true. While he raged at
      them and reviled them for opposing him with the speech of the honest and
      true, it had scratched his stony heart, and he had perceived the
      powerlessness of all his wealth to buy them if he had addressed himself to
      the attempt. So, even while he was their griping taskmaster and never gave
      them a good word, he had written their names down in his will. So, even
      while it was his daily declaration that he mistrusted all mankind—and
      sorely indeed he did mistrust all who bore any resemblance to himself—he
      was as certain that these two people, surviving him, would be trustworthy
      in all things from the greatest to the least, as he was that he must
